quizzes.stem: A web service handles each request in an async function that calls the synchronous SDK client, and under load every endpoint, including those that never ask the model anything, becomes slow together. What is the cause?

options.a: A blocking wait holds the event loop, so other tasks cannot run until it returns
options.b: All handlers share one client, so each model call queues behind the others
options.c: An event loop can serve only one request at a time, so async handlers cannot overlap
options.d: Each model call keeps a processor busy, so the whole server runs short of CPU time

explanation.a: The page says a call that waits "without yielding stops the loop, and every other task waits with it".
explanation.b: Ruled out because one shared client is the advice, not the fault: each client has "a connection pool and thread pools that are better shared between requests".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "one thread with an event loop overlaps thousands of waits", as long as each wait yields.
explanation.d: Ruled out because a waiting call does no computing: the program "waits for the reply while the CPU is idle".

quizzes.stem: A nightly job starts one call for each of 8,000 tickets at once with a bare gather. It sees a wave of 429 errors and loses the labels of the tickets that succeeded because the gather raised. Which change is best?

options.a: Split the tickets into two gathers of 4,000 and run them in turn, one after the other
options.b: Keep the bare gather, and retry each 429 at once inside the task that got it
options.c: Cap the work in flight, and record each outcome in its slot, failures included
options.d: Lower each request's timeout, and catch what the gather raises to keep its labels

explanation.c: The page asks to "bound the calls in flight" and to "collect every outcome, in input order, and decide about the failures afterwards".
explanation.b: Ruled out because a bare gather over a queue "turns a batch into a burst", and an instant retry adds to that burst.
explanation.a: Ruled out because two gathers of 4,000 are still two bursts, and in the page's words "Promise.all and a bare gather give up on the others when one fails", so each half repeats the loss.
explanation.d: is ruled out because, once a bare gather raises, "the results of the others are not returned to you", and a shorter timeout does not bound the burst.

quizzes.stem: A team's client sends bursts of requests at the start of every minute and gets 429 errors, although the daily total is far below the limit. What explains the refusals?

options.a: Cached prompt reads count toward the input limit, so each burst exceeds it
options.b: Capacity comes back gradually, so a spike uses it up before it is restored
options.c: The provider counts the `max_tokens` setting of each request toward output tokens
options.d: Capacity is shared with other organisations, so peaks collide with theirs

explanation.b: The page says the limit is "a bucket that refills continuously, not a counter that resets on the minute", so a spike drains it.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "only uncached input counts toward ITPM" for most models, and cache reads are not counted.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the `max_tokens` setting "does not factor into OTPM rate limit calculations".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the limits are set per organisation: "per organisation and per model class".

quizzes.stem: A job reads a very large file and starts one call per row before it processes any result, and the process runs out of memory. Which design is best?

options.a: Write each result out as soon as its call returns so that memory is freed
options.b: Read all the rows first but start the calls in groups of a hundred rows
options.c: Compress the rows in memory so that more of them fit before the calls start
options.d: Set up eight workers that each take a new item when their own is done

explanation.d: The page's mechanism is "take the next item only when there is room for it", with a worker pool that has "at most limit workers".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "reading them all first puts the file in memory", and groups do not change that.
explanation.c: Ruled out because compression keeps every row in memory and leaves "starts every call at once" in place.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the rows, not the results, fill memory here, and a job "should take a line only when a worker is free", which writing results out sooner does not bring about.

quizzes.stem: Twelve tickets are sent together, and the provider refuses one with a 429. The team wants fewer refusals. What comes first?

options.a: Put a semaphore in front of the calls so that only a few are in flight
options.b: Raise the retry count so that each refusal is repeated sooner than before
options.c: Send the work through more clients so that each one carries fewer calls
options.d: Honour the retry-after header on each 429 before the next request goes out

explanation.a: The page's order is "Bound and pace first; retry last", and the bound "needs no knowledge of the limits and removes the worst bursts".
explanation.b: Ruled out because "retrying a burst you could have avoided spends the time and the quota twice".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page says "Don't create more than one client in the same application", since each has its own pools.
explanation.d: Ruled out because retry with back-off on a 429 "is the last line, not the first".

quizzes.stem: A pipeline's first stage outpaces the stage behind it, and memory grows during long runs. Which fix is best?

options.a: Give the process more memory so that the buffer can hold the whole run
options.b: Run more workers in the first stage so that it finishes its share sooner
options.c: Limit the buffer between the two so that a full one slows the producer
options.d: Spill the buffer to disk so that the growing backlog no longer fills memory

explanation.c: The page says "bound the queue between them: a full queue makes the model stage wait".
explanation.b: Ruled out because a faster first stage only widens the gap: "a fast producer and a slow consumer meet in an unbounded buffer".
explanation.a: Ruled out because "the buffer is your memory".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the slow stage "must slow the stage in front of it instead of letting work pile up", on disk or in memory.

quizzes.stem: Each request takes about four seconds, and a worker pool keeps at most eight in flight. About how many can the pool complete in a minute?

explanation.b: Little's law says "the number of requests in flight equals the request rate times the time each takes", so eight in flight over four seconds is a rate of two a second, about 120 a minute.
explanation.a: Ruled out because it multiplies the bound by the call time, while the page's own case divides: with 6-second calls, "A bound of 20 would cap you at about 200 a minute".
explanation.c: Ruled out because a worker holds its slot for the whole call before it takes another: "run the work, store the result, repeat".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the pool overlaps its calls instead of running them one by one: "Concurrency means starting the next request during that wait".

quizzes.stem: One ticket in a gathered batch fails with a bad request while the others succeed. Under this module's rule for independent work, what does the caller get back?

options.a: Only the successes, listed in the order in which they finished running
options.b: Cancelled siblings and the first error raised to the caller of the batch
options.c: The successes in input order, with no entry kept for the failed ticket
options.d: An error record in its slot, with every other answer kept in order

explanation.d: The pool "returns one outcome per item in input order" and "lets one failure stand alone".
explanation.b: Ruled out because that is what a bare gather does, and "rejects on the first rejection" loses the rest.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the failure keeps its place, as in a list "in which a failure is an exception object in its slot".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the pool "returns one outcome per item in input order".
